title: Small frustrations stay in my head longer than they should.
dek: I notice friction before I have language for it. Then I keep picking at it until the experience makes sense.

panels.title: My extension box had one job.
paragraphs: It kept falling off my bedside table whenever I moved in my sleep. Deeply irritating. So I taped it down, adjusted the placement, and finally stopped thinking about it.

That is very me. If something feels inconvenient or unnecessarily difficult, my brain refuses to let it stay vague. I start asking: why does this feel annoying, why does this take more effort than it should, and how could this be simpler?
panels.pullQuote: Over time, I realized this way of thinking had a name: UX.
panels.afterQuote: Spacing changes readability. Button placement changes behavior. One confusing interaction can make an entire product feel broken even when the code is technically working. That changed how I looked at software: not as just code, but as a series of decisions shaping someone's experience moment by moment.

panels.title: The kind of engineer I want to be.
paragraphs: It also shaped the kind of engineer I want to be. I respect engineers who can say, "I don't know yet," ask better questions, take feedback without making it weird, and care more about solving the problem correctly than protecting their ego.

panels.title: It never felt random.
paragraphs: Every technical decision affects how a real person experiences a product. I like that immediacy. A small change can instantly make something clearer, calmer, faster, or easier to trust.
Frontend did not feel like a random specialization. It felt like the natural result of how I already thought, long before I knew what UX even was.
